questions.q: Meena has moved from a small farming village near Sitapur to Lucknow city to study. Using the chapter's description of rural and urban areas, write four differences she is likely to notice, one on each of: (a) the number of people, (b) the kinds of work and businesses, (c) transport and communication, and (d) who looks after local development.
questions.a: (a) Her village usually has a lower population, while the city has a concentration of human populations. (b) The village has a larger number of agriculture-based occupations and fewer businesses; the city has different kinds of businesses and occupations. (c) The village generally has less elaborate transport and communication systems; the city often has elaborate ones. (d) The village is governed by a gram panchayat; the city has elected local bodies responsible for developing infrastructure and other amenities.

(b) Village: more agriculture-based occupations and fewer businesses; city: different kinds of businesses and occupations
(c) Village: less elaborate transport and communication; city: often elaborate systems
(d) Village: gram panchayat; city: elected local bodies responsible for infrastructure and amenities

Village Rampura has 2,400 people over 8 sq km and village Sonapur has 2,400 people over 4 sq km.
(a) Find the population density of each village.
(b) If 600 more people settle in Rampura and its area stays the same, will Rampura become more crowded than Sonapur? Show the working.
questions.a: (a) Rampura: 2,400 / 8 = 300 people per sq km; Sonapur: 2,400 / 4 = 600 people per sq km. (b) No. Rampura would have 3,000 / 8 = 375 people per sq km, which is still less than Sonapur's 600.
s: (a) Finds 300 per sq km for Rampura and 600 per sq km for Sonapur
(b) Finds 3,000 / 8 = 375 per sq km and concludes it is still less crowded than Sonapur

questions.q: True or False? 'Population density tells us how many people live per unit of area, and it is usually expressed as the number of people per square kilometre.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says demographers assess the number of people living per unit of area, called population density, usually expressed as people per square kilometre (total population divided by area in sq km).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: density is the number of people per unit of area, usually per sq km, found by dividing population by area

questions.q:
A town in Haryana (illustrative data) is deciding where to run a new bus service. Its Sector A has 54,000 people living over 6 sq km. Its Sector B has 60,000 people living over 12 sq km. The town's officers want to know which sector is more crowded, not just which has more people, before they decide.
(a) Write the formula for population density.
(b) Find the population density of Sector A.
(c) Find the population density of Sector B.
(d) A satellite view of one sector shows a grey built-up network of buildings; the other shows large blocks of green and brown land. Which view most likely belongs to Sector B? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Population density = total population of a region / area of the region in sq km. (b) 54,000 / 6 = 9,000 people per sq km. (c) 60,000 / 12 = 5,000 people per sq km. (d) The view with large blocks of green and brown open land, because Sector B is less densely settled (5,000 against 9,000 people per sq km) even though it has more people; open land points to sparser settlement.
s: (a) Density = total population / area in sq km
(b) Sector A: 9,000 people per sq km
(c) Sector B: 5,000 people per sq km
(d) Sector B matches the open green and brown land, as it is less densely settled

questions.q: Two satellite images of the same area in Haryana are taken ten years apart. In the later image, large blocks of green and brown land have turned into a grey network of buildings. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.a: The area has most likely become more densely settled
o: The area has most likely become more densely settled
The area's population must now be above 5,000
The exact population density can now be read from the image
The area must have lost people as its farmland has gone

questions.q: A city has three wards (illustrative data). Ward A: 90,000 people over 15 sq km. Ward B: 48,000 people over 6 sq km. Ward C: 1,20,000 people over 24 sq km. A councillor says, 'Ward C has the most people, so it must be the most crowded and should get the new park first.' Test the councillor's claim.
questions.a: Densities: Ward A 90,000 / 15 = 6,000; Ward B 48,000 / 6 = 8,000; Ward C 1,20,000 / 24 = 5,000 people per sq km. Ward B, with the fewest people, is the most crowded and Ward C is the least crowded. The claim is wrong: crowding is shown by population density (people per sq km), not by the total population, so on that basis Ward B should get the park first.
s: Finds the densities 6,000, 8,000 and 5,000 people per sq km
Identifies Ward B as most crowded and Ward C as least crowded
Rejects the claim: crowding depends on people per unit of area, not on total population

(d) Around 2025, about how many out of every 100 people in India lived in rural areas?

questions.a: (a) The population shift from rural to urban areas and the corresponding decrease in the proportion of people living in rural areas. (b) 68 - 55 = 13 percentage points. (c) 40 - 17 = 23 percentage points. (d) About 100 - 40 = 60 out of every 100. (e) Kolkata and New Delhi.

(b) 13 percentage points (55 to 68)
(c) 23 percentage points (17 to about 40)
(d) About 60 out of 100
(e) Kolkata and New Delhi

questions.q:
A Class 8 group from Pune visits Mumbai in 2026. Their notes read: 'The Gateway of India and the Taj Hotel stand by the sea and are full of tourists. At the Bandra Kurla Complex we saw banks, corporate offices and financial institutions. The Bandra Worli Sea Link joins western and southern Mumbai, and the Coastal Road gives faster connectivity between areas.' The teacher asks how Mumbai became such an economic hub.
(a) What feature of Mumbai's location made it a vital port city?
(b) Which institution set up in 1875 made Mumbai the financial capital, and how many years before the visit was that?
(c) Which place in the notes best shows Mumbai's role as a financial capital today?
(d) Rohan says, 'Mumbai grew only because of its port.' Do you agree? Give a reason using two later developments from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Its location along the Arabian Sea, which made it a port for domestic and international trade. (b) The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE); 2026 - 1875 = 151 years. (c) The Bandra Kurla Complex, with its banks, corporate offices and financial institutions. (d) Only partly. The port gave it trade, but the BSE made it the financial capital, talent from all sections of society gathered there and the exchange of ideas led to innovation; the film industry began in the 1910s and was flourishing by the 1930s, and modern infrastructure now supports a wide range of economic activities.
s: (a) Location along the Arabian Sea, making it a port for trade
(b) The Bombay Stock Exchange, 151 years before 2026
(c) The Bandra Kurla Complex
(d) Partly agrees and gives two later developments such as the BSE drawing talent and ideas, the film industry, or modern infrastructure

questions.q:
Sagarpur is an imaginary port city (illustrative data) that wants to follow Mumbai's example. It has Rs 900 crore and two aims: (1) faster connectivity between areas of the city, and (2) attracting banks and financial institutions. Four projects are offered: a sea bridge (Rs 600 crore), a coastal highway (Rs 450 crore), a business complex with offices for banks (Rs 350 crore) and a seafront promenade for tourists (Rs 250 crore).
(a) Name the Mumbai example in the chapter that matches the sea bridge and the coastal highway, and what each does.
(b) Name the Mumbai examples that match the business complex and the promenade.
(c) Find which pairs of projects fit within Rs 900 crore.
(d) Which pair meets both aims? Justify.
(e) Will this plan alone make Sagarpur a financial capital like Mumbai? Evaluate using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Bandra Worli Sea Link, which connects western and southern Mumbai, reduces traffic jams and eases mobility; the Coastal Road, which enables faster connectivity between areas. (b) The Bandra Kurla Complex, with banks, corporate offices and financial institutions; the Taj Hotel and Gateway of India, famous tourist attractions. (c) Highway + complex = 800, bridge + promenade = 850, highway + promenade = 700, complex + promenade = 600 all fit; bridge + complex = 950 and bridge + highway = 1,050 do not. (d) The coastal highway with the business complex (Rs 800 crore): the highway gives faster connectivity and the complex draws banks; the only other pair with the complex that fits uses the promenade, which does nothing for connectivity, and the bridge with the complex costs Rs 950 crore. (e) Not on its own. In the chapter Mumbai became the financial capital through the Bombay Stock Exchange of 1875, which expanded trade and drew talent from all sections of society, with ideas leading to innovation; infrastructure helps a wide range of activities but does not by itself create that role.
s: (a) Sea bridge matches the Bandra Worli Sea Link (reduces traffic jams, eases mobility); highway matches the Coastal Road (faster connectivity)
(b) Business complex matches the Bandra Kurla Complex; promenade matches the Gateway of India and Taj Hotel tourist area
(c) Works out the pair totals and which are within Rs 900 crore
(d) Chooses the coastal highway with the business complex (Rs 800 crore) as the only pair meeting both aims
(e) Judges that infrastructure alone is not enough, using the Bombay Stock Exchange, talent and ideas

questions.q:
A garment exporter (illustrative data) needs a warehouse and office from which to serve customers across India. The monthly cost of operations would be Rs 42 lakh in Mumbai, Rs 26 lakh in Nagpur and Rs 30 lakh in Ludhiana. If the warehouse is in a city that the chapter names for textile production, buying cloth locally saves Rs 5 lakh a month in transport.
(a) Which of the three cities does the chapter name for textile production?
(b) Find the monthly cost for each city after any saving.
(c) How much a year would the cheapest city save compared with Mumbai?
(d) Which city should the exporter choose? Justify using the chapter's reasons and your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Ludhiana (named with Tirupur for textile production). (b) Mumbai Rs 42 lakh; Nagpur Rs 26 lakh; Ludhiana 30 - 5 = Rs 25 lakh. (c) (42 - 25) x 12 = Rs 204 lakh, that is Rs 2 crore 4 lakh a year. (d) Ludhiana: it is cheapest by Rs 1 lakh a month (Rs 12 lakh a year) over Nagpur because it is a textile centre. Nagpur is close behind because, as the chapter says, growing cities like Nagpur have a lower cost of operations than larger cities; Mumbai, a large metropolis, costs the most.
s: (a) Ludhiana
(b) Monthly costs Rs 42 lakh, Rs 26 lakh and Rs 25 lakh
(c) Yearly saving of Rs 204 lakh (Rs 2 crore 4 lakh)
(d) Chooses Ludhiana as cheapest because of the textile saving, noting that Nagpur is close behind as a lower-cost city and Mumbai costs most

Better roads, highways and the metro rail system instead boosted the expansion of the National Capital Region, which helped ease that pressure.
s: Verdict: False

questions.q: For a class display, a student writes four timeline cards on Delhi. Card 1: 'Delhi has been a centre of culture, trade and administration since the Iron Age.' Card 2: 'The Mughals introduced railways and electricity in Delhi.' Card 3: 'After Independence, ministries, universities and research centres drew people to New Delhi from across the country.' Card 4: 'Gurugram became a major IT and BPO hub in the 1970s.' Say whether each card is correct, and correct any card that is wrong.
questions.a: Card 1 is correct: the chapter says Delhi has thrived as a centre of culture, trade and administration from the Iron Age. Card 2 is wrong: the Rajputs, Turks and Mughals built forts, roads and markets; it was the British who introduced railways and electricity. Card 3 is correct: New Delhi, as capital of the Indian Republic, drew people for jobs and education. Card 4 is wrong: Gurugram has been a major IT and BPO hub since the 1990s.
s: Card 1: correct
Card 2: wrong; the British introduced railways and electricity (the Mughals built forts, roads and markets)
Card 3: correct
Card 4: wrong; Gurugram became an IT and BPO hub since the 1990s

questions.q:
Ravi lives in Ghaziabad and works in central Delhi (illustrative data). By road each trip takes 80 minutes; by metro it takes 50 minutes. He makes 2 trips a day for 22 working days a month.
(a) How many hours a month does the metro save him?
(b) Which statement in the chapter does the metro's role here support?
(c) Explain how such links could help ease the pressure on Delhi's own housing.
questions.a: (a) Saving per trip = 80 - 50 = 30 minutes; 30 x 2 x 22 = 1,320 minutes = 22 hours a month. (b) The chapter says better roads, highways and the metro rail system boosted the expansion of the National Capital Region. (c) When towns such as Ghaziabad and NOIDA are well linked, people can live there and still work in Delhi, so fewer need housing, water and sewerage inside Delhi; the chapter says creating the NCR to include NOIDA and Ghaziabad helped ease the pressure.
s: (a) 30 x 2 x 22 = 1,320 minutes = 22 hours
(b) Metro rail, roads and highways boosted the NCR's expansion
(c) People can live in NCR towns like Ghaziabad and work in Delhi, easing the pressure on Delhi's housing

questions.q: Kolkata's culture appears in the chapter through the Indian Museum and through Durga Puja. Compare the two: (a) what each one is and where it comes from, (b) how often or how long each is part of city life, and (c) what the two together show about a city's culture.
questions.a: (a) The Indian Museum is an institution from the era when Kolkata was the capital of British-ruled India; Durga Puja is an annual festival celebrated by the people. (b) The museum is a permanent building that still stands today; Durga Puja is a five-day festival held every autumn, and in 2021 it was inscribed on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. (c) A city's culture has layers: institutions left by its history and living traditions that its people celebrate together.
s: (a) Museum: an institution from British-era Kolkata; Durga Puja: an annual festival
(b) Museum: permanent, still there; Durga Puja: five days every autumn, UNESCO-listed in 2021
(c) Shows a city's culture combines historical institutions and living, shared traditions

questions.q: A student writes: 'A city's culture is made only by its old monuments and buildings.' Evaluate this statement in five points, using the chapter's examples of cities as cultural hubs, and end with your verdict.
questions.a: (1) Partly supported: Kolkata still has the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial from the time it was the capital of British-ruled India. (2) But vada pav shows culture made by people: a Maharashtrian-style potato dumpling in a Portuguese pav that became popular among Mumbai's textile mill workers. (3) Durga Puja is a living five-day festival every autumn, recognised in 2021 as Intangible Cultural Heritage, not a building. (4) Cities draw people from many regions, creating a potpourri of languages, customs, traditions, food and festivals that are shared in shared spaces. (5) Cities also create cultural centres, libraries, museums, stadiums and gathering spaces, and Fig. 7.17 includes street art, an open-air music festival and commuters interacting, which help people interact, build relationships and form networks. Verdict: the statement is too narrow; monuments are only one part of a city's culture.
s: Accepts the part supported by Kolkata's Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial
Uses vada pav to show culture made by people mixing influences
Uses Durga Puja as an intangible, living tradition
Explains the potpourri created when people from many regions share spaces
Uses facilities and gatherings (street art, music festival, commuters) and gives the verdict that the statement is too narrow

questions.q:
A school in NOIDA (illustrative data) records the AQI each morning for one week in November: Monday 380, Tuesday 410, Wednesday 455, Thursday 430, Friday 395, Saturday 470, Sunday 440. The sports teacher must decide whether to hold outdoor practice on some days or move it indoors for the whole week. The chapter gives a safe limit of 50 for the AQI.
(a) What does the AQI report, according to the chapter's glossary?
(b) On how many days was the AQI over 400?
(c) On the worst day, how many times the safe limit was the AQI?
(d) Should practice be held outdoors on the days at or below 400, or moved indoors for the whole week? Justify with the data.
questions.a: (a) It is a numerical scale that reports air quality by combining data on pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide into a single value; the higher it is, the greater the pollution and the risk to public health. (b) 5 days (Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, Sunday). (c) 470 / 50 = 9.4 times. (d) Indoors for the whole week: even the best day, Monday at 380, is 380 / 50 = 7.6 times the safe limit, and Friday's 395 is 7.9 times, so every day carries a serious health risk; being under 400 does not make the air safe.
s: (a) A numerical scale combining pollutant data into one value; higher means more pollution and health risk
(b) 5 days
(c) 9.4 times
(d) Moves practice indoors all week, showing even 380 is 7.6 times the safe limit

questions.q: Fig. 7.18 shows some challenges faced by Indian cities, including traffic jams, urban slums, waste generation, water scarcity and flooding during monsoons. Using the chapter, (a) give the conditions it names that lie behind traffic jams; (b) give the reason it gives for the growth of slums; (c) give the condition it links to rising waste problems in fast-growing areas; (d) give the causes it names for Bengaluru's water crisis; (e) name the other challenge in Fig. 7.18 that the chapter traces, in Bengaluru, to the same poor urban planning, and say what this shows.
questions.a: (a) Narrow and poorly maintained roads and a growing number of vehicles on the road. (b) A lack of enough affordable housing for everyone migrating to the city, so settlements grow where vacant land is available. (c) The rapid development of unplanned residential areas with poor access to water, sanitation, energy and waste management, as large populations flow in. (d) Overuse of groundwater, lack of rainwater harvesting and encroachment of lake beds, with rapid urbanisation cutting the lakes from around 1,000 to about 200. (e) Flooding during the monsoon; Bengaluru faces both summer water shortages and monsoon flooding due to poor urban planning, which shows that one weakness, poor planning, can cause two opposite-looking problems.
s: (a) Narrow, poorly maintained roads and a growing number of vehicles
(b) Lack of enough affordable housing for migrants
(c) Unplanned residential areas with poor access to waste management and other services
(d) Overuse of groundwater, no rainwater harvesting and encroachment of lake beds
(e) Flooding during the monsoon, traced with water shortage to poor urban planning

questions.q: Singapore has very little land for its people. Explain three ways in which, according to the chapter, it uses its limited land while staying green and easy to live in.
questions.a: (1) Sustainable high-rise buildings with rooftop and vertical gardens, which earned it the title of a 'garden city', reduce heat in summer and support biodiversity. (2) Mixed-use spaces where homes, offices and recreational spaces such as parks and museums are close by; Marina Bay Sands and Raffles Place are only a few kilometres apart. (3) A mass public transport system connecting rail, buses, cycling paths and green walking corridors, which reduces reliance on cars and encourages walking.

questions.q:
Narmadapur, an imaginary riverside town in Gujarat (illustrative data), has Rs 100 crore to redevelop its riverfront. Plan P: a pedestrian-and-cycle bridge (Rs 45 crore) and a riverside walkway (Rs 50 crore). Plan Q: a car flyover across the river (Rs 70 crore) and a parking lot (Rs 30 crore). A survey finds 6,000 people cross the river daily on foot or by cycle, and 2,500 by car.
(a) According to the chapter, what do urban redevelopment projects need to integrate? Name two.
(b) Which bridge on Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront is like the bridge in Plan P, and who can use it?
(c) Find the crossing cost per daily user for the Plan P bridge and for the Plan Q flyover.
(d) Which plan should the town choose? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Any two of: technology, citizen participation, efficient infrastructure, and improved urban services such as waste management, water supply, public transport, energy efficiency, housing and e-governance. (b) The Atal Bridge, which allows pedestrians and cyclists to walk along the river. (c) Bridge: Rs 45 crore / 6,000 = Rs 75,000 per daily user; flyover: Rs 70 crore / 2,500 = Rs 2,80,000 per daily user. (d) Plan P: it serves more than twice as many daily users at about a quarter of the cost per user, fits the budget (Rs 95 crore), and, like the Sabarmati Riverfront and the Atal Bridge, blends public utility with spaces for walking and cycling.
s: (a) Two of technology, citizen participation, efficient infrastructure, improved urban services
(b) The Atal Bridge, for pedestrians and cyclists
(c) Rs 75,000 per user for the bridge and Rs 2,80,000 per user for the flyover
(d) Chooses Plan P using the cost per user and the Sabarmati example

questions.q:
A state plans a new town of 12 sq km (illustrative data) and wants to copy Singapore's density of over 8,000 people per sq km.
(a) At 8,000 people per sq km, how many people would the town hold?
(b) If one quarter of the land is kept for parks and nobody lives there, what is the density of the remaining land? Round to the nearest whole number.
(c) Name two features the chapter says let Singapore keep a high quality of life despite its density.
(d) Singapore's Concept Plan looks up to 40 years ahead and its Master Plan is updated every 5 years. How many Master Plan updates fall within one Concept Plan period, and why does this make planning flexible?
(e) Should the state copy Singapore's density without also copying its planning? Evaluate.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 8,000 = 96,000 people. (b) Land left = 12 - 3 = 9 sq km; 96,000 / 9 = about 10,667 people per sq km. (c) Any two of: mixed-use spaces; a mass public transport system with cycling paths and green walking corridors; sustainable high-rise buildings with rooftop and vertical gardens; senior housing integrated with healthcare, childcare and green spaces; walkability. (d) 40 / 5 = 8 updates; each update reflects the changing needs of the city's infrastructure, so the plan can change as the city changes. (e) No. Singapore manages to grow while keeping a high quality of life despite its density only because of its long-term Concept Plan, Master Plans updated every 5 years and its transport, green buildings and mixed-use design; copying the density alone would bring the crowding pressures the chapter describes for cities, such as strained housing, water and roads.
s: (a) 96,000 people
(b) About 10,667 people per sq km on 9 sq km
(c) Two Singapore features such as mixed-use spaces, mass transport or green high-rises
(d) 8 updates; regular updates reflect changing needs, making the plan flexible
(e) Judges that density without the planning would bring crowding problems, and justifies with the chapter
